extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or advanced high-school students of geometry; readers learning projective geometry, conics, and the axiomatic method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and foundational criteria for defining and developing geometry: metric and projective definitions of conics, projective invariants (cross-ratio, duality), constructive methods, and desiderata for axiomatic systems (simplicity, consistency, completeness, independence, physical correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse focal (metric) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipse is defined as the geometrical locus of all points P in the plane the sum of whose distances, PF1 + PF2, from two fixed points F1, F2 (the foci) has a constant value. (If the two foci coincide the figure is a circle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a metric definition making essential use of distance; Dandelin spheres give a projective proof that a conic section cut from a cone is an ellipse with those foci (PF1 + PF2 = constant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola focal (metric) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperbola is defined as the locus of all points P in the plane for which the absolute difference of distances to two fixed points (the foci) is equal to a fixed constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a metric criterion analogous to the ellipse. The Dandelin-sphere construction with spheres in opposite portions of the cone yields the focal property for the hyperbola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola focal/directrix definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A parabola is defined as the geometrical locus of all points P for which the distance r to a fixed point F (the focus) is equal to the distance to a given line l (the directrix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again a metric definition; in projective terms it is the intermediate case when the cutting plane is parallel to a generator of the cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic (analytic) characterization of conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Any curve defined analytically by a general second-degree equation ax^2 + by^2 + cxy + dx + ey + f = 0 is either one of the three conics, a straight line, a pair of straight lines, a point, or imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, by choosing suitable coordinates any conic can be written in second-degree form; proofs typically use coordinate transformations from analytic geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective definition of conic (projection of a circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conic is the projection of a circle on a plane: projecting a circle C from a point O gives, as intersection with another plane, an ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola according to the position of the plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This projective definition emphasizes properties invariant under projection and leads to a purely projective characterization (and to constructions via projective pencils).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective invariance principle for conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Any property of the circle that is invariant under projection will also be possessed by any conic (i.e., is projectively invariant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to transfer circle-properties (e.g., cross-ratio invariance of four points seen from a fifth) to arbitrary conics by projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio invariance on a conic (points)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any four given points A, B, C, D of a conic K are joined to a fifth point O of K by lines a, b, c, d, then the value of the cross-ratio (a b c d) is independent of the position of O on K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental projective theorem for conics (dual to the line/ tangent statement); a converse holds: if two points O,O' see every quadruple with the same cross-ratio, then the curve is a conic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio invariance for tangents (line-curve form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross-ratio of the points of intersection of any four fixed tangents to a conic with a fifth tangent is the same for every position of the fifth tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by projecting back to the circle where the tangent-angle relations are elementary; supports dual constructions of conics as line-curves (sets of tangents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conic as locus from two projectively related pencils
rubrics_metrics.description: A conic K is the locus of the intersections of corresponding lines of two projectively related pencils (sets of lines through two points 0 and 0' on K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a purely projective construction and explains degenerate cases (e.g., locus may become a straight line or pair of lines) and special types (circle, equilateral hyperbola) when pencils have additional relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conic as a line-curve (dual construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarded as a set of tangents, a conic consists of lines joining corresponding points of two projectively related ranges of points on two fixed tangents; thus 'point-conic' and 'line-conic' are dual notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the dual viewpoint: the tangent at a point is the dual element of the point; duality transforms point-statements into line-statements (e.g., Pascal ↔ Brianchon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-point determination of a conic (constructive criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given five points on an unknown conic (with appropriate non-degeneracy conditions), the conic is determined and further points/intersections can be constructed (exercise: construct D where a line through O meets the conic given 0,0',A,B,C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses matching rays between the two pencils and equating cross-ratios (projective correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Dandelin spheres to derive focal properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce spheres tangent to the cutting plane and to the cone; join an arbitrary point P of the conic to the foci obtained via tangency to show PF1 + PF2 = constant (ellipse) or the analogous relation for hyperbola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric construction connects the metric focal definitions with the conic-as-section-of-cone viewpoint; it is a recommended method to relate metric and projective descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of duality in projective geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: If in the statement of any theorem concerning points, lines, and conics each element is replaced by its dual (point ↔ line, point-on-conic ↔ tangent), the resulting statement is also true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlies the pairing Pascal's theorem ↔ Brianchon's theorem and allows generation of valid dual statements systematically; proofs dualize the sequence of axioms used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desiderata for axiomatic systems: simplicity, economy
rubrics_metrics.description: For an axiomatic presentation one should select a number of (preferably few, simple, and plausible) statements from which other theorems follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of axioms makes the system more useful; the text warns that excessive postulates or complex axioms reduce clarity and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desideratum for axioms: consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulates must be consistent, in the sense that no two theorems deducible from them can be mutually contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalists seek proofs of consistency (or models) for their axioms; paradoxes in set theory and foundational debates motivate careful consistency analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desideratum for axioms: completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of axioms should be complete, so that every theorem of the system is deducible from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes controversy about completeness and the limits posed by results showing completeness and consistency may not be provable within strictly closed systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desideratum for axioms: independence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that the postulates be independent, in the sense that no one of them is a logical consequence of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's work on geometry is cited as an exhaustive study of independence, consistency, and completeness; independence avoids redundancy in the axiom set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undefined primitives and implicit definition by axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiomatic system necessarily contains undefined concepts (e.g., 'point', 'line'); their mathematical meaning is given implicitly by the relations stated in the axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These primitives need not have concrete physical referents for pure mathematics, though for applications correspondence to physical objects is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of axioms to physical reality for applications
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications it is important that the concepts and axioms of geometry correspond well with physically verifiable statements about 'real,' tangible objects (e.g., points as pencil dots, straight lines as stretched threads or rays of light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If formal axioms did not agree more or less with physical properties, geometry would be of little applied interest; experimental precision might require modifying axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of models to demonstrate consistency (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show the consistency of a new geometry (e.g., hyperbolic geometry), build 'models' that satisfy all the axioms of Euclid except the parallel postulate, thereby demonstrating relative consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Klein's model (inspired by Cayley) is cited as a simple model for hyperbolic (Bolyai-Lobachevskian) geometry in which infinitely many 'parallels' exist through an external point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of ordering/betweenness axioms (Pasch's observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain intuitive geometric notions (e.g., ordering/betweenness of points on a line) require explicit axioms (Pasch's axiom: a straight line that intersects one side of a triangle in an interior point must also intersect another side).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect of such details can lead to apparent paradoxes (e.g., faulty 'proofs' that every triangle is isosceles) caused by misuse of poorly specified figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of the parallel postulate and non-Euclidean construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The parallel postulate is independent of the other Euclidean axioms: one can construct a consistent geometry (hyperbolic) in which the parallel axiom does not hold by assuming a contrary postulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical attempts to prove the parallel postulate failed; Bolyai and Lobachevsky developed consistent non-Euclidean geometries, later supported via models (Klein) showing relative consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloid line-family criterion (3D quadric property)
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-sheeted hyperboloid can be defined from three lines in general position: there are infinitely many lines each intersecting all three, forming a surface containing two distinct families of straight lines with specified intersection properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projective property: cross-ratio of the four points where four lines of one family meet a given line of the other family is independent of the latter line's position; the wire-model illustrates non-rigidity (continuous deformations).
